PSE II · Chapter 26

Current, Resistance & Power

Charge in motion

← PSE II Course

26.0 — Setting the Charges in Motion

Chapters 22 through 25 built a complete framework for electrostatics — charges at rest. Charges create fields (Ch 22); Gauss’s Law relates a field to the charge it encloses (Ch 23); potential turns the field into a scalar energy landscape (Ch 24); and a capacitor stores energy in the field between two conductors (Ch 25). In every case the charges, once placed, stayed put.

Chapter 25 ended with a loose end. Connect a charged capacitor to an empty one and the charge is shared, but half the stored energy disappears “to the wires.” That phrase assumed something electrostatics never described: that a wire resists the charge moving through it, and that the resistance turns energy into heat. This chapter makes that precise.

When a potential difference is maintained across a conductor — by a battery, for example — the field inside drives free charges through the material and produces a continuous flow called electric current. This chapter builds the vocabulary of circuits: current, resistance, resistivity, and power.

The story begins with Alessandro Volta (1745–1827), whose voltaic pile first provided a steady potential difference. Before Volta, static electricity gave sparks but no sustained flow. André-Marie Ampère (1775–1836) quickly developed the mathematics of current’s magnetic effects, which return in later chapters. It was Georg Simon Ohm (1789–1854) who connected current to voltage: the current through a conductor is proportional to the potential difference across it. His law, published in 1827, was dismissed as “too simple” to be fundamental, and Ohm lost his teaching position before it was accepted.

“The force of the current in a galvanic circuit is directly as the sum of all the tensions, and inversely as the entire length of the circuit.” — Georg Ohm, Die galvanische Kette (1827)

*Personal note: Ohm’s story is a reminder that simplicity in physics is a feature, not a flaw. His law is one of the most used equations in all of engineering, and it was nearly lost because it seemed “too obvious.”

26.1 — Electric Current

Definition of Current

The electric current \(I\) is the rate at which charge passes through a cross-section of a conductor. If a net charge \(\Delta Q\) crosses in time \(\Delta t\), the average current is \(I_\text{avg} = \Delta Q/\Delta t\), and the instantaneous current is

\[\boxed{\;I \equiv \frac{dQ}{dt}\;}\]

The SI unit is the ampere, \(1\ \text{A} = 1\ \text{C/s}\). The ampere is an SI base unit; the coulomb is defined as the charge carried by 1 A in 1 s.

Direction of Current

Conventional current points the way positive charge would move — from high potential to low, along \(\vec E\). In metals the actual carriers are electrons moving the opposite way. The two descriptions produce identical effects, so conventional current is used throughout.

*Personal note: This convention was set by Benjamin Franklin before the electron was discovered. By the time J.J. Thomson identified the electron in 1897, it was too deeply embedded to change. Every circuit diagram in the world still follows Franklin’s guess.

The current is the same through every cross-section of a single wire. In a steady state, charge cannot pile up anywhere along the wire — if more entered a segment than left it, that segment’s charge would grow without limit and its field would push back until the flows matched. So a wire that narrows, bends or changes material still carries one current along its length. This is charge conservation, and §26.2 uses it immediately.

Current is a flow rate, and Physics I already had one. A fluid of density \(\rho_m\) moving at speed \(v\) through a pipe of area \(A\) carries mass at the rate \(\dot m = \rho_m A v\), and steady flow means \(\rho_m A_1v_1 = \rho_m A_2v_2\) — the continuity equation. The electrical version has the same shape, with charge density \(nq\) in place of \(\rho_m\), and it is derived next.

Fluid flow (Physics I) Charge flow (Ch 26)
Mass flow rate \(\dot m\) (kg/s) Current \(I\) (A = C/s)
Pressure difference Potential difference \(\Delta V\)
Pipe friction Resistance \(R\)
Pump Battery (EMF \(\mathcal{E}\))
\(\dot m = \rho_m A v\) \(I = nqv_dA\)

26.2 — Microscopic Model: Drift Velocity

Charge Carriers in a Conductor

A metal wire holds an enormous number of free electrons — about one per atom in copper. Three quantities describe it:

  • Number density \(n\): mobile carriers per unit volume (m\(^{-3}\))
  • Carrier charge \(q\): for electrons, \(|q| = e = 1.602 \times 10^{-19}\) C
  • Cross-sectional area \(A\) (m\(^2\))

Current from Drift Velocity

The carriers move along the wire with an average drift velocity \(v_d\).

Step 1 — the swept volume. In time \(\Delta t\) each carrier advances \(\Delta x = v_d\Delta t\), so every carrier within that distance of a cross-section crosses it. That region is a cylinder of volume \(Av_d\Delta t\).

Step 2 — count the carriers. At \(n\) per unit volume, the cylinder holds \(N = nAv_d\Delta t\) carriers.

Step 3 — the charge. Each carries \(q\): \(\Delta Q = Nq = nqAv_d\Delta t\).

Step 4 — divide by \(\Delta t\).

\[\boxed{\;I = nqv_dA\;}\]

Dividing by the area gives the current density, the current per unit area:

\[\vec J = nq\vec v_d, \qquad J = \frac{I}{A}\]

\(\vec J\) is a vector that points along the flow of positive charge. For electrons \(q<0\), so \(\vec v_d\) and \(\vec J\) point in opposite directions — the electrons drift against the current, as §26.1 said.

Random Motion vs. Drift

With no applied field the free electrons are far from stationary. They move at thermal speeds of order \(10^6\) m/s, but in random directions, so their average velocity is zero and no charge is transported. An applied field \(\vec E\) exerts \(\vec F = q\vec E\) on each electron, biasing its motion slightly between collisions with the lattice. The result is a small drift superimposed on the random motion.

Example: Drift Speed in a Copper Wire

A 12-gauge copper wire (\(A = 3.31 \times 10^{-6}\) m\(^2\)) carries \(I = 10.0\) A. Copper has mass density \(\rho_m = 8920\) kg/m\(^3\) and molar mass \(M = 0.0635\) kg/mol, with one free electron per atom.

Step 1 — the carrier density. One electron per atom, so \(n\) is the number density of atoms:

\[n = \frac{N_A\rho_m}{M} = \frac{(6.022 \times 10^{23})(8920)}{0.0635} = 8.46 \times 10^{28}\ \text{m}^{-3}\]

Step 2 — solve \(I = nqv_dA\) for the drift speed.

\[v_d = \frac{I}{nqA} = \frac{10.0}{(8.46 \times 10^{28})(1.602 \times 10^{-19})(3.31 \times 10^{-6})}\]

\[\boxed{\;v_d = 2.23 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{m/s} \approx 0.223\ \text{mm/s}\;}\]

Check the scale. That is billions of times slower than the thermal motion, and an electron would need about 75 minutes to drift the length of a 1 m wire. Yet a light comes on the instant the switch closes. What travels fast is the field, not the electrons: closing the switch establishes the field along the whole wire at nearly the speed of light, and every electron in the circuit starts drifting almost at once.

*Personal note: Think of a garden hose already full of water. Open the nozzle and water leaves the far end immediately — not because any molecule travelled the length of the hose, but because the pressure wave did.

Example: A Wire That Narrows

A copper wire of diameter \(2.00\) mm is joined to a section of diameter \(1.00\) mm, and the pair carries \(I = 4.00\) A. Find the drift speed and the current density in each section. (\(n = 8.46 \times 10^{28}\) m\(^{-3}\).)

Step 1 — one current. By the check in §26.1, both sections carry the same \(I = 4.00\) A. Only the area changes.

Step 2 — the areas. \(A_1 = \pi(1.00 \times 10^{-3})^2 = 3.14 \times 10^{-6}\) m\(^2\) and \(A_2 = \pi(0.500 \times 10^{-3})^2 = 7.85 \times 10^{-7}\) m\(^2\).

Step 3 — drift speed and current density.

\[v_{d1} = \frac{I}{nqA_1} = \frac{4.00}{(8.46 \times 10^{28})(1.602 \times 10^{-19})(3.14 \times 10^{-6})} = 9.39 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{m/s}\]

\[J_1 = \frac{I}{A_1} = 1.27 \times 10^{6}\ \text{A/m}^2\]

Halving the diameter quarters the area, so without recomputing:

\[\boxed{\;v_{d2} = 4v_{d1} = 3.76 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{m/s}, \qquad J_2 = 4J_1 = 5.09 \times 10^{6}\ \text{A/m}^2\;}\]

Check against continuity. \(A_1v_{d1} = A_2v_{d2}\), exactly the fluid result \(A_1v_1 = A_2v_2\) — the electrons speed up through the narrow section the way water speeds up through a nozzle. The narrow section needs four times the current density, so it will also need four times the field; §26.3 shows why, and why that section is where a wire heats first.

26.3 — Resistance, Ohm’s Law, and Resistivity

Microscopic Ohm’s Law

For many materials the current density is proportional to the field that drives it:

\[\vec J = \sigma\vec E\]

The constant \(\sigma\) is the conductivity of the material (S/m). This is Ohm’s Law in microscopic form — a statement about a material at a point, not about a device.

From the Material to the Device

Take a uniform conductor of length \(\ell\) and area \(A\) with \(\Delta V\) across its ends.

Step 1 — start at a point. \(J = \sigma E\) holds everywhere inside.

Step 2 — the bridging step: trade \(J\) and \(E\) for device quantities. The current spreads uniformly over the cross-section, so \(J = I/A\). The wire is uniform, so the field is uniform along it, and Chapter 24’s \(\Delta V = -\int\vec E\cdot d\vec s\) collapses to \(\Delta V = E\ell\), giving \(E = \Delta V/\ell\). This is the step that turns a statement about a point into a statement about a component.

Step 3 — substitute.

\[\frac{I}{A} = \sigma\,\frac{\Delta V}{\ell} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \Delta V = \left(\frac{\ell}{\sigma A}\right) I\]

Step 4 — name the bracket. Everything in it is fixed by the material and the geometry, so it is a property of the device, the resistance:

\[\boxed{\;R \equiv \frac{\Delta V}{I}, \qquad \Delta V = IR\;}\]

The unit is the ohm, \(1\ \Omega = 1\) V/A. Writing the material factor as the resistivity \(\rho = 1/\sigma\) (\(\Omega\cdot\)m):

\[\boxed{\;R = \rho\,\frac{\ell}{A}\;}\]

Check the limits, and read the physics off them.

  • Longer \(\ell\) \(\Rightarrow\) larger \(R\). The same \(\Delta V\) is spread over a longer path, so the field — and with it the current density — is smaller.
  • Larger \(A\) \(\Rightarrow\) smaller \(R\). More parallel paths for the same field; the current density is unchanged but there is more area to carry it.
  • \(\ell \to 0\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(R \to 0\). A conductor of zero length drops no voltage — which is why connecting wires are drawn as ideal in circuit diagrams: their \(\ell/A\) is tiny compared with a resistor’s.
  • Back to the narrow wire. At fixed \(I\), the field is \(E = \rho J\), so four times \(J\) needs four times \(E\) — the promise of §26.2, kept.

Area helps a capacitor and hurts a resistor. \(C = \varepsilon_0A/d\) and \(R = \rho\ell/A\) are built the same way — a material constant times a ratio of geometry — but \(A\) sits on opposite sides. More plate area stores more charge per volt; more wire area passes more current per volt, which means less resistance. The same inversion reappears when the two are combined (§26.6).

Ohmic and Non-Ohmic Devices

A device is ohmic if \(R\) is constant — a straight line through the origin on an \(I\) vs. \(\Delta V\) graph. Most metals at fixed temperature are ohmic. Non-ohmic devices — diodes, semiconductors, heated filaments — have a resistance that depends on the voltage or current.

\(\Delta V = IR\) can still define \(R\) at any single point on a non-ohmic curve; what fails is the claim that the same \(R\) holds at every point.

Resistivities of Common Materials

Material Resistivity (\(\Omega \cdot \text{m}\)) Classification
Silver \(1.59 \times 10^{-8}\) Conductor
Copper \(1.7 \times 10^{-8}\) Conductor
Aluminum \(2.82 \times 10^{-8}\) Conductor
Tungsten \(5.6 \times 10^{-8}\) Conductor
Nichrome \(1.00 \times 10^{-6}\) Conductor (alloy)
Carbon \(3.5 \times 10^{-5}\) Semiconductor
Germanium \(0.46\) Semiconductor
Silicon \(2.3 \times 10^{3}\) Semiconductor
Glass \(10^{10}\) to \(10^{14}\) Insulator
Fused quartz \(75 \times 10^{16}\) Insulator

All values at \(20\,^\circ\text{C}\). The range spans roughly 24 orders of magnitude — no other everyday material property varies so widely.

Example: The Resistance of Nichrome Wire

The radius of 22-gauge Nichrome wire is \(0.32\) mm.

(A) Resistance per unit length. Divide \(R = \rho\ell/A\) by \(\ell\):

\[\frac{R}{\ell} = \frac{\rho}{\pi r^2} = \frac{1.00 \times 10^{-6}}{\pi(0.32 \times 10^{-3})^2}\]

\[\boxed{\;\frac{R}{\ell} = 3.1\ \Omega/\text{m}\;}\]

(B) Current with 10 V across 1.0 m. \(R = 3.1\ \Omega\), so

\[I = \frac{\Delta V}{R} = \frac{10}{3.1} = 3.2\ \text{A}\]

Nichrome’s resistivity is about sixty times copper’s, which is why it is the wire inside heating elements: it turns a modest length into a useful resistance.

Example: Stretching a Wire

A wire of resistance \(R_0\) is drawn through a die until it is twice as long. The volume of metal does not change. Find the new resistance.

Step 1 — what is conserved. The volume \(A\ell\) is fixed, so doubling \(\ell\) halves \(A\).

Step 2 — scale each factor of \(R = \rho\ell/A\). The material is unchanged, the length is multiplied by 2, and the area by \(\tfrac12\):

\[R = \rho\,\frac{2\ell_0}{A_0/2} = 4\,\rho\frac{\ell_0}{A_0}\]

\[\boxed{\;R = 4R_0\;}\]

Generalise. Stretching by any factor \(s\) at constant volume gives \(\ell = s\ell_0\) and \(A = A_0/s\), so \(R = s^2R_0\).

Check the limit, and why it is not \(2R_0\). At \(s = 1\) the wire is unchanged and \(R = R_0\), as it must be. The factor is \(s^2\), not \(s\), because stretching attacks \(R\) twice — once through the longer path and again through the thinner one. Reasoning that tracks only the length gets \(2R_0\) and is off by a factor of two.

26.4 — Temperature Dependence and the Drude Model

Temperature Dependence of Resistivity

For most metals, resistivity rises approximately linearly with temperature:

\[\boxed{\;\rho = \rho_0\left[1 + \alpha(T - T_0)\right]\;} \qquad \text{and equivalently} \qquad R = R_0\left[1 + \alpha(T - T_0)\right]\]

where \(\alpha\) is the temperature coefficient of resistivity (\(^\circ\text{C}^{-1}\)). The \(R\) form follows because \(\ell\) and \(A\) change far less with temperature than \(\rho\) does.

Material \(\alpha\) (\(^\circ\text{C}^{-1}\)) Material \(\alpha\) (\(^\circ\text{C}^{-1}\))
Copper \(3.9 \times 10^{-3}\) Carbon \(-0.5 \times 10^{-3}\)
Tungsten \(4.5 \times 10^{-3}\) Germanium \(-48 \times 10^{-3}\)
Nichrome \(0.4 \times 10^{-3}\) Silicon \(-75 \times 10^{-3}\)

Metals (positive \(\alpha\)): higher temperature means stronger lattice vibrations, more scattering, and higher resistivity. Semiconductors (negative \(\alpha\)): higher temperature frees more carriers, which outweighs the extra scattering.

*Personal note: This is why incandescent bulbs draw a surge of current at turn-on. A cold tungsten filament has far lower resistance than a hot one, and the inrush is why bulbs most often burn out the moment you flip the switch.

Example: A Motor Winding as Its Own Thermometer

The copper winding of an electric motor measures \(R_0 = 1.20\ \Omega\) at \(T_0 = 20\,^\circ\text{C}\) before it is switched on. After an hour of running it measures \(1.46\ \Omega\). How hot is the winding?

Step 1 — solve the linear model for \(T\).

\[\frac{R}{R_0} = 1 + \alpha(T - T_0) \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad T = T_0 + \frac{1}{\alpha}\left(\frac{R}{R_0} - 1\right)\]

Step 2 — substitute (\(\alpha_\text{Cu} = 3.9 \times 10^{-3}\ ^\circ\text{C}^{-1}\)):

\[T = 20 + \frac{1}{3.9 \times 10^{-3}}\left(\frac{1.46}{1.20} - 1\right) = 20 + \frac{0.217}{3.9 \times 10^{-3}}\]

\[\boxed{\;T \approx 76\,^\circ\text{C}\;}\]

This is how the temperature inside a sealed winding is measured in practice — no thermometer can reach it, but the winding reports its own temperature through its resistance.

Check the sign and the sensitivity. \(R\) rose, and copper’s \(\alpha\) is positive, so \(T\) must rise — it did. A 22% change in resistance bought a 56 °C change in temperature: because \(\alpha\) is small, modest temperature swings produce small resistance changes, which is why a precision measurement is needed to use a metal this way. A material with a larger \(|\alpha|\) would make a more sensitive thermometer.

The Drude Model

In 1900 Paul Drude modelled the conduction electrons as a classical gas, accelerated by \(\vec E\) and scattered by the lattice ions. The model derives \(\vec J = \sigma\vec E\) rather than assuming it.

Step 1 — between collisions. Each electron feels \(\vec F = q\vec E\) and accelerates at \(\vec a = q\vec E/m_e\).

Step 2 — the bridging step: collisions reset the drift. After each collision an electron’s velocity points in a random direction, so on average it starts from zero drift and gains \(\vec a\,t\) until the next collision. With a mean time \(\tau\) between collisions, the average drift is

\[\vec v_d = \vec a\,\tau = \frac{q\vec E}{m_e}\,\tau\]

This is the step that turns a steadily accelerating particle into a steady flow: the collisions stop the acceleration from accumulating.

Step 3 — substitute into \(\vec J = nq\vec v_d\).

\[\vec J = nq\left(\frac{q\tau}{m_e}\right)\vec E = \left(\frac{nq^2\tau}{m_e}\right)\vec E\]

Step 4 — compare with \(\vec J = \sigma\vec E\).

\[\boxed{\;\sigma = \frac{nq^2\tau}{m_e}\;}\]

Check what it predicts. The conductivity is independent of \(E\), so \(J\) is proportional to \(E\) — Ohm’s Law follows instead of being assumed. More carriers or longer times between collisions raise \(\sigma\); a heavier carrier lowers it. Rising temperature shortens \(\tau\) through stronger lattice vibration, so a metal’s resistivity rises with \(T\) — the positive \(\alpha\) of the table above.

Check the scale. Solving for \(\tau = m_e/(nq^2\rho)\) with aluminum’s \(\rho = 2.82 \times 10^{-8}\ \Omega\cdot\)m and \(n = 1.81 \times 10^{29}\) m\(^{-3}\) (three free electrons per atom) gives \(\tau \approx 7 \times 10^{-15}\) s: some \(10^{14}\) collisions every second. The model is classical and incomplete — quantum mechanics revises the electrons’ speeds — but it gets the form of Ohm’s Law and the order of magnitude of \(\sigma\) right.

Drift is terminal velocity. A constant force opposed by a resistive interaction gives a steady speed proportional to the force — the terminal velocity of Physics I, where drag balances gravity. Here the “drag” is the collisions, and \(v_d \propto E\) is the electrical terminal velocity. That proportionality is Ohm’s Law.

Superconductors

In 1911 Heike Kamerlingh Onnes found that mercury cooled below \(T_c = 4.15\) K has exactly zero resistance — superconductivity. A current set up in a superconducting loop flows indefinitely. The high-temperature cuprate superconductors of the 1980s (YBa\(_2\)Cu\(_3\)O\(_7\) at 92 K, cooled by liquid nitrogen rather than liquid helium) were a revolution. The record at ordinary pressure is 134 K — still far below room temperature, and raising \(T_c\) remains a great open problem.

26.5 — Electrical Power

Power Delivered to a Circuit Element

Step 1 — energy per charge. A charge \(dQ\) that moves through a potential difference \(\Delta V\) changes its potential energy by \(dU = dQ\,\Delta V\) (Ch 24). Across a resistor that energy leaves the charge and goes into the material.

Step 2 — divide by \(dt\). The rate at which energy is delivered is

\[P = \frac{dU}{dt} = \frac{dQ}{dt}\,\Delta V\]

\[\boxed{\;P = I\,\Delta V\;}\]

This holds for any element — a resistor, a motor, a battery being charged.

Step 3 — for a resistor, substitute Ohm’s Law. With \(\Delta V = IR\), or \(I = \Delta V/R\):

\[\boxed{\;P = I^2R = \frac{(\Delta V)^2}{R}\;}\]

All three forms give watts (W = J/s). In a resistor the delivered energy becomes internal energy — the resistor warms — which is called Joule heating.

Which form? The one whose variable is held fixed. The two ohmic forms seem to disagree about whether a larger \(R\) means more or less power. They do not; they describe different circuits.

  • Fixed \(\Delta V\) — a household outlet: \(P = (\Delta V)^2/R\), so a smaller \(R\) draws more power. A 1500 W appliance has less resistance than a 60 W one.
  • Fixed \(I\) — elements in a single loop share one current: \(P = I^2R\), so the larger \(R\) dissipates more. The thin, high-resistance section of a wire is where it heats first.

This is where Chapter 25’s missing energy went. When two capacitors share charge, a surge of current flows through the connecting wires, and the wires dissipate \(I^2R\) for as long as it flows. The lost energy is the integral of that power over the brief surge. Remarkably, the total does not depend on \(R\): a smaller resistance gives a larger, shorter surge, and the energy lost is the same — set only by the charge-sharing, exactly as §25.5 found.

In Physics I, power was \(P = Fv\): force times the rate of motion. \(P = I\Delta V\) has the same structure — the electrical “push” per charge, times the rate at which charge moves.

Example: Power in an Electric Heater

A heater applies \(120\) V across Nichrome wire with \(R = 8.00\ \Omega\).

Step 1 — the current.

\[I = \frac{\Delta V}{R} = \frac{120}{8.00} = 15.0\ \text{A}\]

Step 2 — the power.

\[P = I^2R = (15.0)^2(8.00)\]

\[\boxed{\;P = 1.80\ \text{kW}\;}\]

Check with the other form: \((\Delta V)^2/R = (120)^2/8.00 = 1.80\) kW. A typical space heater — all of it converted to internal energy.

The Kilowatt-Hour

The kilowatt-hour is the energy unit on electricity bills: \(1\ \text{kWh} = (1000\ \text{W})(3600\ \text{s}) = 3.6 \times 10^6\) J. Despite its name it is a unit of energy — power multiplied by time.

Example: Why Power Lines Run at High Voltage

A power station delivers \(P = 10.0\) MW through transmission lines of total resistance \(R_\text{line} = 5.00\ \Omega\). Compare the power lost in the lines when it transmits at \(10.0\) kV and at \(100\) kV.

Step 1 — the current is set by the delivered power. \(P = I\Delta V\), so \(I = P/\Delta V\).

\[I_{10} = \frac{10.0 \times 10^6}{10.0 \times 10^3} = 1000\ \text{A} \qquad I_{100} = \frac{10.0 \times 10^6}{100 \times 10^3} = 100\ \text{A}\]

Step 2 — the loss is \(I^2R\) in the lines.

\[P_{\text{loss},10} = (1000)^2(5.00) = 5.00\ \text{MW} \qquad P_{\text{loss},100} = (100)^2(5.00) = 50.0\ \text{kW}\]

\[\boxed{\;\text{Ten times the voltage} \;\Rightarrow\; \text{one hundredth the line loss: } 50\% \to 0.5\%\;}\]

Check the scaling. \(P_\text{loss} = I^2R_\text{line} = (P/\Delta V)^2R_\text{line}\), so at fixed delivered power the loss goes as \(1/(\Delta V)^2\). The line resistance did not change; the current did. This is why transmission lines operate at hundreds of kilovolts and transformers step the voltage down near where the power is used.

Note which voltage appears here: the transmission voltage fixes the current. It is not the voltage drop across the line — using \((\Delta V)^2/R_\text{line}\) with 100 kV would predict a loss far larger than the power delivered.

26.6 — Summary

Key Concepts

  1. Electric current \(I = dQ/dt\) is the rate of charge flow, in amperes (A = C/s). Conventional current points the way positive charge moves. In a steady state the current is the same through every cross-section of a wire.

  2. Drift velocity: \(I = nqv_dA\), \(\vec J = nq\vec v_d\). Drift speeds are tiny (a fraction of a mm/s in copper); the field that drives them is established at nearly the speed of light.

  3. Ohm’s Law: microscopically \(\vec J = \sigma\vec E\); for a device \(\Delta V = IR\). A device is ohmic when \(R\) is constant.

  4. Resistivity: \(R = \rho\ell/A\). Resistivity is a material property that spans 24 orders of magnitude. Stretching a wire at constant volume scales \(R\) by the square of the stretch.

  5. Temperature: \(\rho = \rho_0[1 + \alpha(T - T_0)]\). Metals have positive \(\alpha\); semiconductors negative.

  6. Drude model: \(\sigma = nq^2\tau/m_e\). Collisions turn a steady force into a steady drift, which is why Ohm’s Law holds.

  7. Power: \(P = I\Delta V\) for any element; \(P = I^2R = (\Delta V)^2/R\) for a resistor. Use the form whose variable is held fixed. Transmission losses fall as \(1/(\Delta V)^2\).

Looking Ahead

Chapter 27 introduces DC circuits — networks of resistors and batteries, analysed with Kirchhoff’s rules, which are charge conservation and energy conservation written for a circuit. It derives the series and parallel rules for resistors (and shows why they are the reverse of the capacitor rules) and then brings capacitors and resistors together in RC circuits, where the time constant \(\tau = RC\) governs exponential charging and discharging.

*With current and resistance in hand, we now have the vocabulary to read a circuit diagram. Kirchhoff’s rules will give us the grammar.
